planting.note: Plant on a slope or berm in fall in truly fast-draining sand or decomposed granite, away from lawn runoff; prune lightly after spring bloom to keep the wand-like form tidy.

directions: A true desert-rock-garden sage, this species carries fine silvery, scalloped foliage on wand-like stems topped with small white flower whorls, excellent for extreme-drainage xeriscapes where showier chaparral sages rot out. Clay or regular irrigation kills it quickly, so excellent drainage is non-negotiable. Combine it with other Colorado and Mojave desert scrub natives rather than mesic garden beds.

planting.note: Plant in fall into gravelly wash or slope conditions with excellent drainage; expect foliage thinning during extreme heat, which is normal stress-deciduous behavior, not plant failure.

directions: Blue-to-rose flower color variation on a single species gives real planting flexibility, and an unusually long bloom window from April into November extends hummingbird forage well past spring for a desert sage. Give it the gravelly wash and slope conditions of its native Colorado Desert range. Works well massed in a low-desert rock garden with palo verde or brittlebush rather than as a standalone specimen.

planting.note: Plant in fall into a small rock garden or container with excellent drainage even in wetter coastal climates, where it can be overwatered by rainfall alone.

directions: One of the smallest, tidiest native sages, this true one-to-two-foot mounding shrub is ideal for small rock gardens and containers where larger relatives would be oversized, with unusual pale-blue flowers against bright, fuzzy green rather than gray foliage. It is notably less drought-tough than other desert sages and benefits from an occasional light water in summer rather than being left bone-dry. Avoid heavy clay.

planting.note: Plant in fall within roughly ten miles of the coast for fog influence; tolerates sandy or clay soils with fast, medium, or slow drainage. Prune to shape in late summer or early fall after bloom.

directions: A fast-growing, fragrant, fountain-forming coastal shrub with a large, showy lavender-blue flower display, this Channel Island and Baja endemic is one of the few native sages genuinely suited to large-scale coastal hedging or screening rather than just rock gardens. It is adapted to fog influence and performs poorly in hot interior gardens, so restrict it to near-coastal sites. It is unusually forgiving of soil type for a native sage, tolerating both sandy and clay ground.

planting.note: Divide rooted runners in spring, or plant cuttings, into low-fertility, well-drained rocky soil under high desert tree canopy or on a shaded slope; give it room to spread as a groundcover.

directions: A genuine shade-tolerant native sage, this species fills a sage-for-shade niche that none of the full-sun chaparral and desert sages can, spreading by underground runners as a flowering groundcover under trees in dry rocky soil. It is one of the only native western sages that actually prefers shade over sun. Deer and rabbit resistant, it works well used intentionally as a groundcover rather than planted as a single specimen.

planting.note: Plant in fall with light shade in hot low-desert gardens, or full sun at higher and cooler elevations; water moderately to establish, then reduce.

directions: An unusually adaptable native shrub, this sage blooms reddish-pink from spring through fall in either sun or shade, with aromatic minty-citrus foliage that makes it a long-season hummingbird plant for Southwest gardens that doesn't demand full blasting sun like most native sages. Native to dry, rocky canyon slopes in southern Arizona's sky islands, it handles more cold and more garden soil types than lowland desert sages. It makes a good transitional plant between a xeriscape bed and a part-shade native border.
